nodes.name: Cu2O Nanocubes Synthesis
nodes.procedure: 1.5 mmol of CuSO4·5H2O and 0.5 mmol of C6H5Na3O7 were dispersed in 80 mL of deionized water. Then, 20 mL of 1.25 M NaOH and 50 mL of 0.03 M C6H8O6 were sequentially added to this solution. The mixture was stirred for approximately 30 min until it turned orange-red. Finally, the Cu2O nanocubes (Cu2O NCs) were obtained through centrifugation, washing, and drying.

nodes.name: Fe/Co Hydroxide Nanoflower Synthesis
nodes.procedure: 80 mg of Cu2O NCs, 2 g of PVP, 22 mg of CoCl2·6H2O, and 22 mg of FeCl3 were dispersed in a 160 mL mixture of deionized water and ethanol (1:1 v/v). Afterward, 64 mL of 1 M Na2S2O3 was rapidly added to the solution. The Fe(OH)3/Co(OH)2 nanoflower clusters were obtained by hydrothermal reaction, followed by centrifugation and washing with deionized water and ethanol.

nodes.name: High-temperature Phosphatization
nodes.procedure: Finally, sodium hypophosphite and Fe(OH)3/Co(OH)2 (in a 10:1 ratio) were placed in a tube furnace under N2. The mixture underwent phosphatization at 350 °C for 2 h, followed by natural cooling to room temperature, resulting in the formation of Fe2P/CoP hollow nanoflowers (Fe–CoP nanoFCs).

nodes.characterization_summary: Fe–CoP nanoFC exhibits hollow nanoflower cluster structure with shell layer of approximately 50 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figs. S5 and S6 present SEM images of Fe(OH)₃, Co(OH)₂, and Fe(OH)₃/Co(OH)₂ and the phosphatization product of Fe(OH)₃/Co(OH)₂ (Fe–CoP nanoFC) (Fig. 1b–c). The images reveal that Fe(OH)₃/Co(OH)₂ has a hollow nanoflower cluster structure, and the phosphated products retain the morphology of its precursor.

properties.description: SEM of Fe-Co PFC showing nanocube morphology

nodes.characterization_summary: Fe–CoP nanoFC shows hollow structure with shell layer of ~50 nm; elements Fe, Co, P, O evenly dispersed in shell layer.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 1d shows the hollow structure of the Fe–CoP nanoFC. Fe–CoP primarily exists in a shell layer of approximately 50 nm. Fig. 1e–h illustrate the dispersion of Fe, Co, P and O across the Fe–CoP nanoFC.

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS confirms presence of Fe, Co, P, O evenly dispersed in Fe–CoP nanoFC shell layer with partial oxygen residues.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The results indicate that all the elements are evenly dispersed within the shell layer. EDS analysis confirmed the presence of partial oxygen residues, which may have resulted from the decomposition of hydroxides at high temperatures.

nodes.characterization_summary: HR-TEM shows lattice fringes at 0.205 nm, 0.224 nm, 0.196 nm, 0.254 nm corresponding to Fe₂P (201), (111) and CoP (112), (200) planes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The HR-TEM image in Fig. 1i shows the rich nanocrystalline material on the Fe–CoP nanoFC shell. Further magnification of the localized region reveals the interlocking presence of four types of lattice fringes (Fig. 1j) with distances of 0.205 nm, 0.224 nm, 0.196 nm, and 0.254 nm, which are equivalent to the Fe₂P (201) and (111) crystal planes and the CoP (112) and (200) crystal planes, respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: SAED shows concentric rings corresponding to CoP (311), (020), (111) and Fe₂P (111) planes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Additionally, electron diffraction of the selected regions (SAED) (Fig. 1k) revealed concentric rings corresponding to the CoP (311), (020), and (111) planes and the Fe₂P (111) plane.

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD of Fe–CoP nanoFC shows characteristic CoP peaks; no obvious Fe₂P or Fe(OH)₃ peaks detected.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 2a displays the XRD patterns of the Cu₂O NCs, Fe(OH)₃/Co(OH)₂, and Fe–CoP nanoFC. ... Fortunately, characteristic CoP peaks were observed in the spectrum of the Fe–CoP nanoFC, indicating the successful phosphatization of Co(OH)₂. Notably, the characteristic peaks of Fe₂P and Fe(OH)₃ are absent from the spectra of the Fe–CoP nanoFC.

nodes.characterization_summary: Fe–CoP nanoFC has specific surface area of 53.2 m²/g and mesoporous structure of ~40 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 2b shows that the BET results indicate a specific surface area for the Fe–CoP nanoFC (53.2 m² g⁻¹), approximately 21 times greater than that of the Cu₂O template due to its hollow structure and flower-like clusters. The results of the pore size distribution indicate a mesoporous structure of ~40 nm in the Fe–CoP nanoFC.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS confirms presence of Co–P bonds (Co 2p at 778.58 eV, 793.27 eV), Fe–P bond (Fe 2p at 707.10 eV, weaker), with CoP dominating and Fe₂P nanocrystals; O 1s shows O–Fe (530.26 eV), O–Co (531.14 eV), O–P (532.35 eV); P 2p shows P 2p3/2 (130.00 eV), P 2p1/2 (130.90 eV), P–O (134.00 eV).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The fine spectrum of Co 2p in Fig. 2c can be decomposed into four groups of characteristic peaks. ... the peaks at 778.58 eV and 793.27 eV correspond to Co–P bonds, confirming the existence of CoP in the catalyst. The Fe 2p fine spectrum in Fig. 2d shows ... a prominent peak at 707.10 eV is equivalent to the Fe–P bond. The fine spectrum of O 1s in Fig. 2e can be broken down into four characteristic peaks: O–Fe (530.26 eV), O–Co (531.14 eV), O–P (532.35 eV)... The fine spectrum of P 2p in Fig. 2f can be similarly assigned to the characteristic peaks of P 2p3/2 (130.00 eV), P 2p1/2 (130.90 eV), and P–O (134.00 eV) bonds.

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-14h stability test SEM shows Fe–CoP nanoFC largely retains granular structure with less defined contours and some agglomeration.
nodes.evidence_snippet: To further validate the excellent stability of Fe–CoP nanoFC, we conducted SEM (Fig. S17)... As shown in Fig. S17, after 14 h of galvanostatic polarization, the catalyst largely retained its granular structure, although its contours became less defined, and some agglomeration was observed.

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-14h stability test XRD shows Fe–CoP nanoFC phase composition remains predominantly CoP (PDF No. 29–0497) with slightly less pronounced characteristic peaks.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. S18 reveals that the overall phase composition of Fe–CoP nanoFC remained predominantly CoP (PDF No. 29–0497) post-stability testing, though the characteristic peaks became slightly less pronounced.

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-14h stability test XPS shows chemical bonding and relative elemental composition of Fe–CoP nanoFC remained largely unchanged (Fig. S19, Table S6).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. S19 and Table S6 further show that the chemical bonding and relative elemental composition of Fe–CoP nanoFC remained largely unchanged.
